explainer.heading: What the article says
explainer.body: Author Susan Freinkel wrote down everything she touched for a day: 196 of 298 things were plastic. This began her book “Plastic: A Toxic Love Story”. The article explains plastic’s history, its benefits and its harm, and concludes that plastic itself is not bad — the way we use it is the problem.

explainer.heading: History
explainer.body: The first plastic, Bakelite, was invented in 1907 by Leo Baekeland, who marketed it as the “material of a thousand uses” (radios, combs, jewellery). It inspired artificial substitutes for natural materials such as ivory, whose animals were becoming endangered. In the 1920s–30s plastics were used for packaging, clocks and clothing; during World War II plastic filled the gap when natural resources were not sufficient.

explainer.heading: Benefits
explainer.body: Plastic packets keep food fresh longer than metal, glass or paper; plastic bottles are unbreakable; disposable gloves and instruments prevent infection in hospitals. Vehicles with plastic parts are lighter and use less fuel; light packaging needs less energy to ship; plastics made solar panels possible.

explainer.heading: Harm
explainer.body: More than nine billion tons have been made since the 1950s; production may double in 20 years. Very little is recycled, and plastic does not break down. Chemicals from landfills enter ground water and the sea, are eaten by marine life and eventually by us. Every ocean has plastic pollution and over 260 animal species are affected.

explainer.heading: Solutions
explainer.body: Some plastics (e.g. hospital supplies) are worthwhile, but plastic bags and straws are hard to justify — many countries have banned them. We can choose products made of metal, wood or glass, which are easier to recycle or dispose of.

explainer.heading: Vocabulary
explainer.body: Expressions with take / have / get / keep: take for granted, have an effect, get rid of, keep in mind. Easily confused words: affect/effect, lose/loose, advice/advise. Words beginning with out- / up-: outnumber, outgrow, upgrade, upset, outcome.
explainer.example: We take plastic for granted because it is everywhere.

explainer.heading: Grammar: kinds of sentences (1)
explainer.body: Declarative (statement) ends with a full stop: “Plastic does not break down.” Interrogative (question) ends with “?”: “Should plastic be banned?”

explainer.heading: Writing: an essay
explainer.body: Title, introduction (topic + your view), body paragraphs (one main idea each with examples — e.g. benefits, harms, solutions), conclusion summing up. Use linking words: firstly, however, moreover, in conclusion.

questions.q: Give two benefits of plastic mentioned in the article.
questions.model: Plastic packets keep food fresh longer, and disposable plastic hospital equipment prevents the spread of infection. (Also: unbreakable bottles; lighter vehicles use less fuel; solar panels.)

questions.q: Why is it difficult to get rid of plastic?
questions.model: Plastic does not break down over time; the same qualities that make it long-lasting make it hard to dispose of. Very little is recycled, so most is thrown away.

questions.q: “Plastic might be doing more harm than good.” Discuss using points from the article, and suggest ways to tackle the problem.
questions.model: Plastic is useful: it keeps food fresh, makes unbreakable bottles, prevents infection in hospitals and makes vehicles lighter and solar panels possible. But over nine billion tons have been made, very little is recycled and it does not break down. Its chemicals reach ground water and the sea, harming marine life and us; every ocean is polluted and over 260 species are affected. To tackle this we can stop using plastic bags and straws, choose metal, wood or glass products, and use plastic only where it is truly needed, like hospital supplies.
points: Pollution of water/oceans, animals and humans affected
Solutions: bans on bags/straws, alternatives, use wisely
